items.title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.original_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_description: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer Claims ITL Editorial Team Tue, 10/06/2026 - 11:19 Chief claims officers must transform their departments into AI-native ground-truth engines or risk becoming the bottleneck in enterprise transformation. October 7, 2026 Image For decades, the mandate of the chief claims cfficer was relatively clear: build a strong organization to investigate claims, control costs, manage litigation, negotiate settlements, and deliver fair outcomes. That mandate is no longer sufficient. The 2027 chief claims officer has a much bigger job: build the insurer's ground-truth engine—an AI-native operation that produces superior outcomes, industrializes negotiation excellence, and converts what claims learns into intelligence for the entire enterprise. This is not simply about using AI to make legacy claims processes more efficient. AI is turning insurance into an information business—and the most important ground truth in that business is generated in claims. Claims reveal what actually happened to the risks the insurer underwrote, what drove the loss, and what ultimately determined its economic outcome. To compete in an AI world, insurers will need to capture that ground truth, make it machine-readable, and use it to improve underwriting, pricing, reserving, and portfolio management. That puts claims—and the chief claims officer—on the front line of this unprecedented transformation. A new competitive environment Claims officers in traditional claims organizations face urgent and pressing competition from two sources at once. On one side is an increasingly industrialized plaintiff bar. On the other side is a new generation of AI-native insurers, poised to move forward. On the first side, consider Morgan & Morgan. The personal-injury giant says it has invested roughly $300 million in technology and AI and plans at least $1 billion more over the next decade. Its proprietary MX2 platform supports medical-record extraction, case research, document generation, demand letters, and trial preparation, while Injury.com digitally acquires and qualifies potential claims. Private equity is adding fuel, investing in personal-injury platforms to scale technology, analytics, marketing and standardized operations. The plaintiff bar is turning claim development and negotiation from individual craftsmanship into an industrial system. On the second side, a new generation of AI-native insurers is being built without decades of legacy technology, workflows and organizational baggage. Companies such as Corgi are attempting to build insurance businesses from inception around modern data architectures, AI agents and technology-speed iteration. McKinsey has warned that AI-native insurance businesses can increasingly build and refine products in weeks while incumbents remain calibrated to annual planning cycles and multi-year transformations. Legacy insurers are being squeezed from both directions: out-innovated by the plaintiff bar in the contest over outcomes and potentially out-architected by AI-native insurers in the contest over how insurance itself operates. Claims sits directly in the middle. That changes the requirements of its leader. 1. Level the playing field with the plaintiff bar The plaintiff bar has largely approached AI as a weapon for improving economic outcomes. Carriers have largely approached it as a tool for workflow efficiency. AI-powered demand packages are working. Carriers are only beginning to experiment seriously with the corresponding AI-powered offer package. Meanwhile, sophisticated plaintiff organizations are accumulating data, developing proprietary AI and attracting enormous capital. The plaintiff bar is both the threat and the proof point. They are investing their own money—and increasing institutional capital—because better case development, persuasion, and negotiation improve their economics. The CCO must build institutional capabilities that can match increasingly industrialized counterparties. 2. Institutionalize negotiation excellence Most carriers have some excellent negotiators. That is no longer enough. If negotiation materially affects indemnity outcomes, it cannot remain an individual skill distributed unevenly across thousands of claims professionals. The organization should know who its elite negotiators are, why they outperform and how those behaviors can be replicated. Carriers that cannot identify, measure and reproduce negotiation excellence do not really possess a negotiation capability. They possess individual negotiators. The CCO must turn individual excellence into measurable institutional capability. 3. Stop putting AI band-aids on pre-AI claims operations Many carriers can produce an impressive list of AI-centric projects: summarize a file, extract information, draft correspondence, analyze a demand, route work, search notes, or give adjusters Copilot. Those applications can create real value. But old process plus an AI tool means slightly better old process. McKinsey has warned about layering new technology onto legacy insurance operating models. BCG similarly distinguishes between deploying AI into existing processes and reshaping workflows around AI. The CCO must redesign the operating model, not merely automate the existing one. 4. Build machine-first claims The traditional claim file was built primarily for humans. Documents, notes, emails, medical records, and litigation materials accumulate while experienced professionals gradually construct an understanding of what happened. In an AI-native operation, every claim should progressively become a machine-readable representation of the claim—the people, events, evidence, injuries, allegations, relationships, negotiations and outcomes. That structured claim becomes the substrate on which specialized AI agents can continuously reason. Instead of occasionally asking AI to summarize a file, machines continuously read, structure, monitor, compare, detect, and prepare. The CCO must make claims machine-readable while elevating, not diminishing, human judgment and action. 5. Build and lead a hybrid workforce The future claim officer will have two kinds of capacity at their disposal: human expertise and machine intelligence. AI agents will increasingly read, structure, monitor, research, compare, detect, analyze and prepare. Humans will increasingly concentrate on judgment, investigation, strategy, creativity, empathy, supervision, accountability and negotiation. That will make exceptional claims professionals more important, not less. Imagine an elite negotiator supported by agents that continuously understand the evidence, medical history, venue, plaintiff counsel, negotiation history, and comparable outcomes. The machine handles much of the cognitive preparation. The human concentrates on what exceptional humans do best: think, strategize, persuade, read the counterparty, exercise judgment, and negotiate. The CCO must become the architect of human and machine capacity—designing how each works together to produce better outcomes. 6. Make every negotiation a learning event A sophisticated plaintiff demand should eventually meet an equally sophisticated carrier response. But the bigger opportunity comes afterward. Every demand, analysis, strategy, offer, response, counteroffer, and outcome must become institutional knowledge in the same way that the plaintiff bar is institutionalizing these events. Which plaintiff firms consistently outperform? Which strategies work against them? Which facts change settlement value? Which negotiators outperform expectations? Where does the organization systematically overpay? Every negotiation should make the next negotiation smarter. The CCO must ensure every claim and negotiation makes the organization smarter. 7. Elevate claims into the insurer's ground-truth engine This is where the transformation extends beyond claims. Underwriting begins with hypotheses about risk. Pricing quantifies them. Reserving updates them. Claims discovers what was actually true. Claims learns what caused the loss, how injuries developed, what evidence mattered, how attorneys behaved, which defenses and negotiation strategies worked, and what the risk ultimately cost. Yet much of that knowledge remains trapped in PDFs, notes, litigation files and the heads of experienced claims professionals. Claims should continuously produce structured intelligence that flows into underwriting, pricing, reserving, risk, reinsurance and portfolio management. The claim is no longer simply something to resolve and close. It is one of the insurer's richest proprietary information assets. The CCO must turn claims knowledge into enterprise intelligence—making the claims organization the feedback loop that allows the entire enterprise to learn. 8. Don't let claims become the transformation bottleneck This may be the requirement that matters most to the rest of the C-suite. A legacy insurer can modernize distribution, underwriting, pricing and portfolio management. But if its richest source of ground truth remains trapped inside a document-centric, human-first claims operation moving through multi-year transformation cycles, the rest of the enterprise eventually hits a wall. AI-native competitors do not have to unwind decades of organizational architecture before redesigning how humans, machines and data work together. Incumbents do. That makes speed itself a competitive capability. The modern CCO must protect the integrity of a massive, consequential operation while simultaneously making it capable of continuous change. The plaintiff bar is moving at technology speed. AI-native competitors are being built for technology speed. Claims cannot continue moving at insurance speed. The CCO must ensure claims leads rather than constrains the insurer's AI transformation. The mandate has changed None of these requirements eliminates the traditional responsibilities of the CCO. Claims still must be handled fairly; customers, regulatory obligations, litigation, reserves and operational discipline still matter. But those responsibilities are increasingly table stakes. Sophisticated plaintiff organizations are industrializing the pursuit of settlement dollars while AI-native insurers are being architected as technology-speed information businesses. Between them sits a claims organization that, at many incumbents, was designed for another era. That creates both a threat and an extraordinary opportunity. Carriers that generate that ground truth better, negotiate from it more effectively, make it machine-readable and distribute it throughout the enterprise will possess something more valuable than a more efficient claims department. They will possess a continuously learning insurance enterprise. As chief claims officers enter 2027, the question is no longer whether their departments will use more AI. It is whether they can transform their departments into a competitive advantage rather than the bottleneck preventing the enterprise from changing with it. Taylor Smith John Burge

items.rss_description: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/05/2026 - 17:40 The employment report for September in the U.S. showed a loss of 7,000 jobs in financial services. Insurance, alone, has now lost 90,000 jobs since May 2025. What's going on? I have a theory, and it's not about artificial intelligence. If I'm right, hiring in insurance will stay in the doldrums for a while. Let's have a look. As Insurance Business reports , the industry still employs a massive 2.9 million people in the U.S., but claims jobs are down a hefty 21% over the past year, while life and health is off 4%, P&C down 1.7%, and agents and brokers down 1.1%. The losses are accelerating: The article says, " Insurers lost about 1,900 jobs a month on average in 2025 and roughly 6,900 a month so far in 2026." A thorough analysis in Barron's mostly attributes the job losses to cost-cutting under pressure. Barron's notes that the surge in rates following the COVID disruption has slowed. In addition, government subsidies for healthcare have been cut even as claims costs keep increasing. In the face of pressure on both premiums and expenses, insurers have had to become more efficient, Barron's says. It does say AI has played a role by automating tasks but doesn't treat that as a huge issue just yet (and I've been arguing for months that the fears of job losses to AI are overstated). You could also add the effects of the "silver tsunami" -- the oft-quoted projection by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in 2021 that 400,000 insurance professionals would retire by the end of 2026. Unemployment in insurance remains well below that for the economy writ large -- 3.1%, vs. 4.2% -- so some of the job losses may simply be that companies haven't yet been able to fill the positions left by retirements. But I think there's an overarching issue that gets short shrift if you spend too much time in the details. My Theory My theory boils down to uncertainty. I think economic and geopolitical uncertainty are holding back the economy, in general, and the insurance industry, in particular. And I don't see the uncertainty subsiding any time soon. Tariffs have not only raised costs but, because of their on-again, off-again nature, have slowed investment and the sort of adaptation of supply chains that would ordinarily happen if, say, Canadian lumber suddenly became 50% more expensive. Why spend a lot of money and time if prices might return to normal shortly, whether because of a court ruling against tariffs, because Democrats win control of Congress and assert its power, or simply because President Trump changed his mind? Now add the uncertainty from the war on Iran. Even though oil flows out of the Middle East are improving, Iran retains the capability to attack tankers, to blow up one of the major pipelines being used to skirt the Strait of Hormuz, or to do more damage to the diesel refineries in the region, whose loss has contributed so much to the soaring prices for the crucial fuel. While Trump has repeatedly told us that Iran wants to make a deal and that prices for oil will soon plummet, some of us are old enough to remember how the Iranian zealots acted after taking 66 American hostages in 1979. Angry at President Carter, they didn't release the hostages until minutes after Ronald Reagan became president in January 1981. Who's to say the Iranian theocrats won't treat Trump the way their predecessors treated Carter, declining to make a deal until he leaves office? What is now looking like a blue wave in next month's midterm elections might relieve some of the uncertainty about tariffs, perhaps even leading to serious settlement talks with Iran, but a loss of control by Trump would surely lead to at least a burst of chaos -- perhaps even a sustained stretch. The Democrats are itching to go after him, and he would surely return fire with every one of the many assets at his disposal. The current uncertainty and the prospects that it will continue will create headwinds for the economy, which insurance, especially P&C, tracks closely. The problem will be even worse than normal, I believe, because the effects will hit personal lines so hard. Replacement costs for cars have surged in recent years because of supply chain disruptions, and they will likely stay in flux. Insurers will also have to deal with possibly significant changes in driver behavior if gasoline and diesel prices stay so high -- or go even higher. Costs for home repairs have likewise soared, and uncertainty will tend to keep them high. Meanwhile, the general uncertainty about the economy has fueled inflation, leading the Fed to raise rates for the first time in years and to signal that it may raise rates again soon. A result has been 7% mortgages that have pretty much crushed the housing sector. The reduction in construction means fewer homes to insure, and the stagnant resale market limits the opportunities to poach customers as homes change hands. The result will, I believe, be unrelenting pressure on revenue and costs at a time when customers are exhausted from all the post-COVID rate increases. I hope I'm wrong, but it's hard to see a lot of hiring in that sort of environment. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The latest jobs report for the U.S. highlighted a surprising decline in employment in insurance. I have a theory about the reason -- and it's not AI. PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited has now reported that its new US $12 million issuance of insurance-linked securities under its Great Wall Re Limited special purpose insurer is actually a quota share reinsurance sidecar, the first in Hong Kong, designed to provide protection to its offshore wind power property insurance book on the Chinese […] PICC P&C’s new $12m Great Wall Re is the first Hong Kong sidecar ILS issuance was published by: www.Artemis.bm Our catastrophe bond deal directory Sign up for our free weekly email newsletter here .
items.extracted_text: PICC P&C’s new $12m Great Wall Re is the first Hong Kong sidecar ILS issuance - Artemis.bm PICC P&C’s new $12m Great Wall Re is the first Hong Kong sidecar ILS issuance - Artemis.bm PICC P&C’s new $12m Great Wall Re is the first Hong Kong sidecar ILS issuance 14th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited has now reported that its new US $12 million issuance of insurance-linked securities under its Great Wall Re Limited special purpose insurer is actually a quota share reinsurance sidecar, the first in Hong Kong, designed to provide protection to its offshore wind power property insurance book on the Chinese Mainland. Given the limited information, we were incorrect in initially reporting that the new Great Wall Re issuance we had learned about was a catastrophe bond, having made the assumption it was a follow-up to PICC Property and Casualty Company’s debut sponsorship back in late 2022, the $32.5 million Great Wall Re Limited cat bond deal. PICC Property and Casualty Company has instead utilised Hong Kong’s insurance-linked securities regulatory regime to become the first collateralised reinsurance sidecar sponsor to use an SPI located there. We had reported on October 5th that a new Great Wall Re issuance of insurance-linked securities had been completed, assuming it to be another cat bond from the sponsor, then following up a few days later after we learned it was a US $12 million (HK $94m) issuance of notes . Now, it’s clear that this is a landmark first quota share reinsurance sidecar securitisation for Hong Kong, as the country successfully expands the use-cases for its ILS infrastructure. This morning PICC Property and Casualty Company has said that the US $12 million (HK $94m) Great Wall Re ILS issuance is “the first issuance of insurance-linked securities with a “sidecar” structure in the Hong Kong market,” and the first issuance of sidecar insurance-linked securities by any domestic Chinese insurance company. It’s a relatively unique deal as well given it provides reinsurance to both PICC People’s Insurance and Property Insurance covering offshore wind power property risks in mainland China, certainly an infrequently seen risk profile for the ILS market, perhaps the first time the market has seen these risks in ILS form. The insurer said this is “another innovative practice for the company to use the international capital market to spread insurance risks after the successful issuance of disaster bonds in Hong Kong in 2022.” Being a sidecar, the underlying subject reinsurance arrangement with this US $12 million Great Wall Re deal is a quota share, or proportional reinsurance, transferring the risks to capital market investors on that basis. The Hong Kong based SPI raises capital to fund the risks by issuing equity or debt securities, with those funds deposited in trust accounts and invested in low-risk, highly liquid assets, paying the investors backed the deal over-time. The income and loss of the insurance-linked securities are linked to the profit and loss of the sidecar’s proportional reinsurance contracts. PICC P&C explained, “Its issuance structure reflects the core characteristics of income sharing, risk sharing and flexible loading and unloading between insurance companies and capital market investors, so it is called “sidecar”. The “sidecar” insurance-linked securities and disaster bonds that spread risks through super-compensation reinsurance complement each other, which provides new tools for Chinese insurance companies to expand risk diversification channels and enhance underwriting capabilities.” PICC P&C further stated, “This issue introduces the risk of China’s offshore wind power insurance into the international capital market, enhances international investors’ understanding of China’s green energy insurance business, and expands the risk diversification channel for the development of green energy for insurance services. “The insurance-linked securities previously issued in the Hong Kong market are all disaster bond structures. This “sidecar” issuance enriches the transaction structure and business scenario of the Hong Kong insurance-linked securities market, which helps to promote the coordinated development of the Hong Kong insurance market, capital market and professional service institutions, and helps improve the Hong Kong International Financial Center. Function, improve the global competitiveness of Hong Kong International Financial Center, and inject new momentum into the financial innovation of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. “In the next step, People’s Insurance and Property Insurance will continue to practice political and people’s requirements, coordinate development and security, deepen the exploration of insurance risk securitization, continuously broaden the risk dispersion channels, improve the risk protection capacity of large disasters, and contribute to the construction of the national disaster risk protection system and the construction of the Hong Kong International Financial Center.” Hong Kong’s Financial Services & Treasury Bureau said that it “welcomed the inaugural issuance of insurance-linked securities (ILS) in the form of a “sidecar” by the PICC Property & Casualty Company (PICC P&C) in Hong Kong.” Secretary for Financial Services & the Treasury Christopher Hui commented, “We welcome PICC P&C’s issuance of Hong Kong’s first ‘sidecar’. This demonstrates Hong Kong’s combined strengths in reinsurance and capital markets. “The issuance marks significant progress gained for Hong Kong’s insurance industry and capital markets in risk transfer and the use of alternative capital under the support of our country. It will further enhance the market’s capacity to manage catastrophe and other specialty risks, and consolidate Hong Kong’s position as an international risk management centre. “This will enable us to unleash the synergy effect of multilayered risk transfer and pooling mechanisms through ILS and other tools, thus consolidating our strategic role as a regional and global catastrophe and specialty risk management hub. “ILS and captive insurance, which we have long been promoting, can provide enterprises ‘going global’ with diversified means of spreading and managing risks. “We expect this combination of financial policy measures will allow enterprises to leverage Hong Kong as a safe haven for ‘going global’ with greater ease of mind.” Clement Cheung, Chief Executive Officer of the Insurance Authority added, “Riding on policy support from the National Financial Regulatory Administration, this ILS issuance fully demonstrates the commitment and determination with which we pursue the development of Hong Kong into a global risk management centre. “The IA will also sustain efforts to facilitate introduction of protected cell company as an ILS structure and review the existing definition of eligible ILS investors for a more vibrant trading market.” Now that we understand this new Great Wall Re insurance-linked securities arrangement for PICC P&C is a quota share reinsurance sidecar deal we have removed it from our catastrophe bond Deal Directory and added it to our directory of reinsurance sidecar transactions . It’s encouraging to see the expansion of Hong Kong’s ILS regime to incorporate sidecar arrangements and also good to see the unique use-case to cover offshore wind power risks in China. Find details of numerous reinsurance sidecar investments and transactions, including life reinsurance sidecar structures, in our directory of collateralized reinsurance sidecar transactions . All of our Artemis Live insurance-linked securities (ILS), catastrophe bonds and reinsurance video content and video interviews can be accessed online. Our Artemis Live podcast can be subscribed to using the typical podcast services providers, including Apple, Google, Spotify and more. Launched in 2008, Leadenhall Capital Partners has built a proven track-record across the ILS market, with strategies focused on reinsurance opportunities, catastrophe bonds, life and alternative credit insurance linked investments. During a recent interview with Artemis around the key conference season, Luca Albertini, CEO and one of the founders of the firm, discussed how he hopes to differentiate Leadenhall to attract clients through the rest of 2026 and into 2027. “We hope investors will see in Leadenhall an established player (we launched in 2008) with access to a deep pool of experience underwriting skills, with a stable senior management team and the support of a large multinational financial services group (MSI), whilst maintaining independence in the investment decisions and a corporate structure (partnership) which strongly aligns the investment team with the interest of our investors,” Albertini told Artemis. Expanding further on this, the CEO then detailed what opportunities he currently sees within the market that Leadenhall can use to grow its business further into 2027 and beyond. “Leadenhall has seen a significant growth in its AUM in 2026, whilst remaining focused on its core offering,” Albertini said. He continued: “The team has capacity to further grow its current offering, but we constantly monitor investor appetite for different products and we assess the opportunity in line with our view of the medium term potential for those opportunities and our own skills set needed to underwrite the underlying products.” Addressing the firm’s technology roadmap, Albertini highlighted how Leadenhall is adopting a measured approach to artificial intelligence, balancing enterprise-wide adoption with strict oversight. “Leadenhall has invested in AI, and is currently having business access to one leading platform . Each team and each function in the firm is challenged to think how to use AI to increase productivity and improve our ability to analyse risk,” the Leadenhall Capital Partners CEO said. Concluding: “We are doing this however in a controlled way and lots of attention is also put on “hallucinations” and on the quality of the output, so the validation of what AI generates remains key.” Read all of our interviews with ILS market and reinsurance sector professionals here . items.title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.original_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_description: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/12/2026 - 17:45 The recent report that auto thefts fell 21% in the U.S. in the first half of the year reminds me of a friend's carjacking some 30 years ago — surely the shortest in history. My overeducated friend, with degrees from Brown and the Sorbonne, had just added a certification as an auto mechanic and liked cars that required constant tinkering. While driving near his home in Washington, DC, one afternoon, he stopped at a stop sign, and a pedestrian motioned to him that he had a question. Tim rolled down his window, and the man shoved a gun in his face, ordering him out of the car. The man got in, engaged the clutch and drove... two feet. He tried again, but the car stalled after two more feet. He tried a third time. A fourth. He hadn't even made it halfway into the intersection before he jumped out, threw the keys at Tim's chest and ran off. I'd never thought of having a diseased clutch as an anti-theft device but have watched with interest over the years as actual devices have continually improved. They've now gotten to the point that, combined with other factors, thefts fell 17% in 2024, tumbled 23% last year, to the lowest levels in decades, and are way down again this year. The good news for insurers is likely to continue, too. Let's have a look. Some of my optimism stems simply from the steady modernization of the car fleet. Even though soaring prices for cars have encouraged people to hold on to cars longer than in the past, older, more vulnerable cars are steadily being retired, and that trend will continue. In the face of public pressure, companies whose cars were most likely to be stolen have also issued software patches and other updates — as a result, the percentage of car thefts of Kias and Hyundais fell to 14% of the total last year, from 16% in 2024 and 21% in 2023, even as the total of thefts dropped precipitously. Meanwhile, the supply chain has sorted itself out post-COVID, so thieves can't rack up the sorts of profits they did from stealing scarce parts in recent years. The U.S. war on Iran may unsettle the supply chain again, including by pushing sales of electric vehicles during a time of high gasoline prices, but the effects have been muted so far, and I suspect they'll remain so. Law enforcement has stepped up efforts to prevent all sorts of crimes, and car thefts are a visible target at just about all levels of policing. I'm not sure how much more severe enforcement can become, but, especially in a fraught political environment, I don't see that anyone will relax. Potentially the most important — but fraught — factor that will determine how much car thefts keep falling relates to surveillance technology. Flock has built a massive business by installing cameras on roads nationwide that take pictures of license plates and respond to, among other things, alerts from police departments about stolen vehicles. There are lots of efforts to also figure out how to knit together all the images being gathered by dashcams, which are currently in about one in 10 vehicles in the U.S. and which are being adopted quickly. Combining all those feeds could provide real-time intelligence for police departments, making it far easier to catch thieves and creating a massive disincentive for them to steal cars in the first place. But.... We've also seen how surveillance can be abused, as I wrote in August . Flock faces a scandal because dozens of police officers used its technology to stalk current and former romantic partners, and the temptation to use surveillance illicitly will only increase as the technology becomes more powerful. My gut tells me that it will take time, perhaps years, to sort through all the tensions between law enforcement and privacy but that we'll eventually get to the point where some severely circumscribed uses of license plate readers will take another cut out of auto thefts. The privacy issue is one we've mostly navigated with Ring cameras and surveillance cameras on building, so there's a blueprint for progress The bad guys are always innovating, just as the good guys are, but I think the favorable glide path for car thefts should continue. Cheers, Paul P.S. My other bizarro car theft story, this one involving a nephew and an odd situation for the adjuster: While my nephew was visiting DC last year, his Hyundai was stolen off the street by four kids — who drove the car right past him as he was talking with the police officer who responded to his report of the crime. They took the car on joy rides for a few days — as evidenced by the thousands of dollars of traffic violations they ran up in DC and Maryland — then used it in a drug deal that went bad. The car wound up full of bullet holes, and a friend of the kids was shot. Panicking, the kids put the badly wounded girl in the trunk of the car and dumped her in front of her high school. These young geniuses then abandoned the car and tried to run off but were promptly apprehended by school security. (The girl healed fine.) The insurance issue was that the adjuster couldn't look at the car because it was in police custody as a crime scene. So my nephew's insurer kept him in a rental car for weeks until it finally satisfied itself that the car was a total loss and wrote him a check for a new one. My nephew spent weeks unwinding the traffic tickets. He actually had to drive to Baltimore from Philadelphia to appear in court and provide evidence that he couldn't have been at the wheel for the moving violations because he wasn't in Maryland when they occurred. Image Paul Carroll Car thefts in the U.S. tumbled to their lowest levels in decades in 2025, and are down a further 21% this year. The trend is likely to continue, too. items.rss_description: TESTING focus newsletter grant Thu, 10/01/2026 - 15:37 some summary here October 1, 2026 View this email in your browser | Forward to a colleague ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. This month, we're focusing on IT Ops: Change Management FROM THE EDITOR Some two decades into the insurance industry's digital transformation, companies have spent hundreds of billions of dollars on new core systems, cloud migrations, digital portals, and AI tools — but the technology was rarely the hardest part. The hardest part was the people. The people part has long been treated as a supporting act in large technology transformations. But as the pace and complexity of transformation accelerates, that approach is showing its limits. Employees nod along, say they're using the new system, and then quietly find workarounds. Leadership mandates adoption from the top while alignment quietly fractures below. Organizations sprint to the go-live date and then discover that the real work hadn't started yet. Samit Bhandari has watched this pattern play out across the P&C insurance industry for 20 years as a partner at PwC. He's worked with carriers of all sizes through core system replacements, AI rollouts, and full-scale digital transformations — and has seen where these programs succeed and where they quietly go off the rails. He acknowledges there has been improvement—he says the assumption that most large technology programs fail is increasingly out of date. But he says organizations keep making a lot of the same, old mistakes, including the tendency to underinvest in what happens after a go-live, to confuse executive messaging with genuine alignment, and to treat transformation as a one-time event rather than a continuous process. Read the full interview to find out what red flags signal a change management program in trouble, why smaller carriers are often better at transformation than their larger counterparts, and what Bhandari thinks the industry has stopped doing that it should start doing again. continue reading > Reducing the Risk in Change Management Paul Carroll There's often a disconnect in technology adoption that goes unnoticed in business. A leader might mandate the use of AI, and employees will say they're using it—but are they really changing the way they do things, or are they just going through the motions to show compliance? How do you get people on the same page in a big technology transformation? Samit Bhandari First, just in terms of getting everyone on the same page, it's the fundamentals of what we've always said about getting stakeholders engaged—executive, top-down engagement early, right? The messaging from that level through various levels of the organization. And then just the strategic, tactical things—the change champion network and the communication early and often. When you bring in AI—we should be more nimble. read the full interview > MORE ON CHANGE MANAGEMENT Change Management Is Changing by Melissa Palmer Change management can no longer be viewed as a one-time project discipline. It must become an organizational capability. Read More How to Put People First in Your AI Rollout by Tracey Brown "We made a deliberate decision to treat employee confidence as the primary KPI of our AI transformation." Read More Insurance Hiring Practices Hamper Transformation (Part 1) by Amy Radin Insurance companies hire for sector expertise, but transformation demands cross-boundary judgment that traditional filters miss. Read More The Answer to Too Much Technology Is More Technology by Riv Arthur Claudeforce signals a shift from building tools for humans to use and toward creating infrastructure where machines increasingly do the work. Read More How to Build Tomorrow's Insurance Workforce by Afiong Ekong Insurance's talent crisis demands a shift from hiring for past experience to identifying transferable skills and future potential. Read More Making Innovation Stick in Insurance Organizations by Abrianne Harmon Sustainable innovation in insurance requires organizations to master change adoption through culture building and strategic training design. items.title: Business Interruption Claims Are Approaching $1M Average
items.original_title: Business Interruption Claims Are Approaching $1M Average
items.rss_title: Business Interruption Claims Are Approaching $1M Average
items.rss_description: The average cost of a business interruption claim is nearing $1 million, an upward trend that appears to have several causes. A new report shows BI losses are being pushed up by natural catastrophes, growing risk in supply chains, rising …
items.extracted_text: Business Interruption Claims Are Approaching $1M Average Article 0 Comments The average cost of a business interruption claim is nearing $1 million, an upward trend that appears to have several causes. A new report shows BI losses are being pushed up by natural catastrophes, growing risk in supply chains, rising geopolitical tensions, inflation costs and technology-related disruptions. An analysis from Allianz Commercial of nearly 8,000 business interruption claims valued at $7.82 billion between 2021 and 2025 shows the average BI claim exceeded $950,000. That figure is 70% higher than the corresponding average property damage claim. Claims frequency has been relatively steady over the last few years, but the average value of claims rose by more than 30% annually in the past two years, according to the report. Related: Judge Throws Out Bulk of Economic Claims Over Baltimore Bridge Tragedy “What we’re seeing isn’t necessarily more claims — it’s that each claim is getting significantly more expensive,” said Melissa Hill, North American head of claims for Allianz Commercial. “The biggest culprit is time. Supply chains are still fragile, and when something breaks, it takes much longer to get parts, materials, and equipment to rebuild. During that extended downtime, inflation is compounding the cost of every single day a business can’t operate.” The most expensive cause of BI claims was fire and explosion, which accounted for more than 40% of the total value of all claims analyzed. Fire was responsible for nine of the 10 costliest man-made business interruption events over the five-year period examined. Natural catastrophes were the second most expensive cause of BI claims by value (34%), and they were the most frequent cause (26%). Machinery breakdown was the third leading cause by value (6%). The report points to concentrated production as a growing BI vulnerability. Many industries rely on a small number of specialized suppliers or facilities. Additionally, “geopolitical tensions” like the wars in Ukraine and Iran, are driving up energy prices and logistics costs and adding pressure to supply chains. Tariffs are impacting losses too, the report shows. “Tariffs are one of those factors that don’t always make headlines in the insurance world, but they’re quietly adding real cost and complexity to claims,” Hill said. “When you impose tariffs on key building materials — take softwood lumber, where 85% of U.S. supply comes from Canada — you’re directly inflating the cost of every rebuild. And in a typical property claim, about 60% of the loss is rebuilding costs, so that impact is substantial.” Tariffs are also creating delays as companies scramble to find alternative suppliers or absorb surcharges. That extends restoration timelines and lengthens the business interruption period, according to Hill. “The net effect is that our loss adjustment process has become more complex, requiring more comprehensive analysis, and that added complexity comes with higher expenses across the board,” she added. The lingering effects of the COVID-19 pandemic may also have contributed to higher BI costs, according to Christopher J. Boggs, president and chief consultant of Boggs Risk & Insurance Consulting. Boggs believes the supply chain disruptions that drove up costs during the pandemic have begun to ease. “Supply chains were a major issue during COVID. I tend to think that has begun to smooth out,” Boggs said. The period studied in the Allianz report began during the early days and the height of the COVID shutdowns. Boggs believes future BI claim costs will be closer to historic norms. “My opinion is that the research over the following five years — Jan. 1, 2026, to Dec. 31, 2030 — will see the cost drop closer to the pre-COVID averages,” he said. “Remember, business income losses are based on the period the business is shut down.” Related: As AI Agents Go Rogue, Cyber Insurers Are Adapting Their Policies Matt Weaver, an attorney with Reed Smith who specializes in insurance recovery, agrees that COVID may have played a role in the BI trends in the report, but he takes a less optimistic view, predicting costs will continue to rise because of economic conditions and global instability. “There’s no stopping the trends in that report,” Weaver said. “You’ve got more global uncertainty in the supply chain, you can see that in what’s happening in the Middle East. You’ve got more concerns about AI. You’ve got, currently, less frequent natural disasters, but when they happen, they’re more severe. There’s been a lot of data about that, especially with hurricanes. So, this notion that business interruption is getting more severe, you’re going to keep seeing that.” The report shows cyber incidents are becoming a growing source of BI losses “as ransomware attacks, cloud outages and software glitches disrupt businesses and ripple through supply chains.” Ransomware was the top cause of cyber-related BI, but other disruptions, including IT outages, flawed software updates and cloud service failures, made up “a meaningful share of large cyber losses,” the report states. More than 48,000 outages were tracked across cloud and software services in 2025, the report shows. Prolonged recovery periods following natural catastrophes were another factor contributing to rising BI costs, according to the report. Many BI claims from Hurricane Helene, which struck in September 2024, remain unresolved because some businesses have taken that long to recover. Supply chain delays, labor shortages and volatile material costs extend recovery periods and increase losses, according to the report. Hill called Hurricane Helene “a textbook example” of long-tail natural catastrophe losses, in which claims were extended by a “cascading effect.” “Helene wiped out critical infrastructure in places like Spruce Pine, North Carolina, which supplies roughly 85% of the world’s high-purity quartz for semiconductors,” Hill said. “You can’t just relocate that kind of specialized production overnight, and the downstream disruption rippled across the global tech supply chain for months.” Bottlenecks arose in rebuilding local infrastructure, including roads, rail, and utilities, she added. “The big takeaway for adjusters is that you have to think beyond the physical repair timeline from day one,” Hill said. “If you’re not accounting for supply chain dependencies and infrastructure recovery in your early estimates, you’re going to be chasing the true loss figure for a very long time.” Because of the increased severity, Weaver sees BI coverage getting more expensive, more restrictive and harder to get. “To the extent companies are using it, they might have higher deductibles or higher waiting periods or other things that that limit what they can actually recover,” he said. “So the industry is going to respond to increased severity how they always respond to increased severity, which is you’re going to have more expensive coverage and you’re going to have less of it.” Was this article valuable? items.extracted_text: In casualty ILS motivations are key, timelines must be realistic: Trahan, Calidris - Artemis.bm In casualty ILS motivations are key, timelines must be realistic: Trahan, Calidris - Artemis.bm In casualty ILS motivations are key, timelines must be realistic: Trahan, Calidris 14th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Casualty insurance-linked securities transactions are complex and require strong alignment, which makes finding strategic partners and understanding their motivations key, while at the same time given the complexity of arrangements such as casualty sidecars, realistic timelines are important, Philippe Trahan of Calidris Investment Partners said yesterday. Trahan, Co-founder and Co-CEO of insurance-focused investment manager Calidris Investment Partners, was speaking during a casualty ILS focused panel session at the ILS Bermuda Convergence 2026 conference yesterday. As a company with a focus on opportunities in these longer-tailed areas of insurance and reinsurance, Trahan noted that Calidris recognises the time required to both get comfortable with counterparties and asset managers involved in casualty transactions, as well as being cognisant of the time needed to get to well-structured and aligned deal outcomes. “What we spend a lot of time on, we’re really more focused on finding partners, establishing strategic partnerships. What we want to avoid is we don’t want to be a hedge. So therefore motivations as to why, whether it’s an MGA or broker facility these days, an insurer or reinsurer that is considering wanting to launch a sidecar, why is it that they’re doing it, and what are their motivations?,” Trahan explained. “What I find is then, it’s a bit of a different approach. I would say it’s a market that was mostly done on a bilateral basis between investors and counterparties, and so this year with the kind of syndicated market, which is a normal and natural evolution, it actually shows that it’s growing, it has legs. “It does bring some additional complexity, and there’s a realisation that’s required on the broker or counterparty side. Once you’re comfortable that their motivations are trying to strive to achieve a partnership, that will ideally be scalable and repeatable, these require a lot of time from the management suite. So they don’t do this for a one-year trade and just disappear. So that’s quite helpful.” He went on to suggest that timelines need to be realistic, as the complexity and work-effort involved in casualty ILS deals means that they are unlikely to be completed particularly quickly. Trahan said, “The other obstacle is, we find, unrealistic timelines. These sidecars take six to 12 months to do, and anyone that comes now with a sidecar wanting to do it by year end, that’s wholly unrealistic timelines in my view, there’s a fair amount of diligence that’s required.” There also needs to be an understanding of the additional complexities that go into structuring and creating a transaction that needs to take into account both the insurance liabilities and asset management sides of the equation. Trahan continued, “There’s a lot of discussion you have with the other side, that is either the securities team of a broker or generally with counterparties, that if they discussed ILS markets in the past, they probably discussed using cash, T-bills as collateral. So starting to discuss CLOs and rated feeder notes, that generally tends to bring a different group within that organisation, or you only end up working with bigger organisations. Or if you’re dealing with an MGA group, you bring fronters into the mix, and that just makes things more complex and just takes more time. That’s another dynamic, another element that we find.” Trahan also discussed the critical importance of alignment in casualty ILS transactions, highlighting that expectations need to be set, particularly around alignment on both the potential upside and downside of any partnership arrangement on casualty risks. He explained, “The last element I would point to is willingness for counterparties to share in the upside and the downside. So having to further strengthen the alignment, sliding scale commissions for example is one of those elements that just show more alignment. Because ultimately they’ll know their book way better than we will. “We’ll spend a lot of time discussing how you come with that view, and then we’ll build in a slide around it. This is not me or you trying to see whether I have a different view, a lower view of your loss ratio, so there’s an asymmetric transaction that takes place. That’s not how we think of it, so that requires more time as well.” Trahan’s comments all speak to the complexity of casualty risks and the structural innovation that has come about through the use of insurance-linked securities technology to enable investors to participate in these areas of insurance. They also highlight the need for a disciplined approach and a willingness to fully-engage with partners on transactions, to avoid any unexpected or uncertain outcomes. October 1, 2026 Image FROM THE EDITOR Some two decades into the insurance industry's digital transformation, companies have spent hundreds of billions of dollars on new core systems, cloud migrations, digital portals, and AI tools — but the technology was rarely the hardest part. The hardest part was the people. The people part has long been treated as a supporting act in large technology transformations. But as the pace and complexity of transformation accelerates, that approach is showing its limits. Employees nod along, say they're using the new system, and then quietly find workarounds. Leadership mandates adoption from the top while alignment quietly fractures below. Organizations sprint to the go-live date and then discover that the real work hadn't started yet. Samit Bhandari has watched this pattern play out across the P&C insurance industry for 20 years as a partner at PwC. He's worked with carriers of all sizes through core system replacements, AI rollouts, and full-scale digital transformations — and has seen where these programs succeed and where they quietly go off the rails. He acknowledges there has been improvement—he says the assumption that most large technology programs fail is increasingly out of date. But he says organizations keep making a lot of the same, old mistakes, including the tendency to underinvest in what happens after a go-live, to confuse executive messaging with genuine alignment, and to treat transformation as a one-time event rather than a continuous process. Read the full interview to find out what red flags signal a change management program in trouble, why smaller carriers are often better at transformation than their larger counterparts, and what Bhandari thinks the industry has stopped doing that it should start doing again. Reducing the Risk in Change Management Paul Carroll There's often a disconnect in technology adoption that goes unnoticed in business. A leader might mandate the use of AI, and employees will say they're using it—but are they really changing the way they do things, or are they just going through the motions to show compliance? How do you get people on the same page in a big technology transformation? Samit Bhandari First, just in terms of getting everyone on the same page, it's the fundamentals of what we've always said about getting stakeholders engaged—executive, top-down engagement early, right? The messaging from that level through various levels of the organization. And then just the strategic, tactical things—the change champion network and the communication early and often. items.extracted_text: Verisk estimates Hurricane Isaias insured onshore property losses in $1bn to $2bn range - Artemis.bm Verisk estimates Hurricane Isaias insured onshore property losses in $1bn to $2bn range - Artemis.bm Verisk estimates Hurricane Isaias insured onshore property losses in $1bn to $2bn range 13th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Verisk, a catastrophe risk modelling and data analytics specialist, has now issued an initial industry insured loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias, saying that onshore property losses from the storm could reach $2 billion. Verisk’s initial industry loss estimate includes losses from wind and privately insured storm surge, as a result of hurricane Isaias’ landfall in the Florida Panhandle. The company added that wind damages are expected to account for the vast majority of insured losses from the storm. Verisk further said that its estimate includes losses to onshore residential, commercial and industrial properties and automobiles for building, contents and time-element coverages, with modeled scenarios that incorporate losses from wind and storm surge. The company expects that losses from precipitation-induced flooding will not be a significant factor with Isaias. Commenting on the damages seen, Verisk added, “The most severe wind damage occurred west of Isaias’ landfall location, particularly in Florida’s Santa Rosa and northeastern Escambia counties. Reported impacts included roof damage, structural damage, downed trees and widespread debris. In Okaloosa County, the most common damage mechanism was trees falling onto residential structures. Overall, the event was characterized primarily by wind-related damage, including fallen trees, damaged roofs, fencing losses and debris impacts. “Power outages were widespread across the Florida Panhandle, with some counties reporting outages affecting a majority of residents. Additional impacts were reported in Alabama and Georgia, where the weakening storm and its remnants caused downed trees and further power disruptions.” This first initial insurance market loss estimate for hurricane Isaias from Verisk is one of the lower available so far, although within the anticipated low to mid single digit billion range. As we reported earlier , Euler ILS Partners, the specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, put an initial insurance industry loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias in the range of $2 billion to $4 billion. Cotality (formerly CoreLogic), estimated that insured losses from wind and storm surge from hurricane Isaias will be in the $2 billion to $3 billion range. items.title: Early planning, documentation key to university property claims: Experts
items.original_title: Early planning, documentation key to university property claims: Experts
items.rss_title: Early planning, documentation key to university property claims: Experts
items.rss_description: Universities should involve claims specialists early and carefully document expenses to maximize business interruption insurance recoveries, presenters said Monday at the University Risk Management & Insurance Association’s annual conference.
items.extracted_text: Sandy Mitchell, director of MIT’s Office of Insurance, said hiring a forensic accountant helped the university recover an additional $616,000 in business interruption-related expenses following a 2015 water damage claim at a student residence. MIT relocated about 100 students to a hotel after a pipe burst in July 2015. Repairs were completed in November, but MIT had contracted to retain the hotel rooms through January, she said. The claim also involved lost rental income and additional expenses for transportation, meal plans, laundry and network services, Ms. Mitchell said. After the loss, MIT clarified its policy wording to cover rental income losses if student housing cannot reopen before the fall semester. “If the policy isn’t really clear on it, try and make the policy clear on it, and get the extra language added if you need to,” she said. MIT also received approximately $10 million in insurance payouts for two machinery losses at its central utility plant in 2015 and 2016. Most of that amount covered business interruption expenses because the university had to purchase electricity from the grid, which costs about $75,000 a day, while the plant was out of service, she said. Physical damage to property of a type insured under the policy, including potentially damage to suppliers’ or utility providers’ property, is required to trigger business interruption coverage, said Charles Doherty, division executive general adjuster at FM. Determining whether costs fall under property damage, business interruption or extra expense coverage can be challenging, particularly when damaged research materials must be replicated, he said. A 2019 transformer fire at Yale University’s Kline Biology Tower disrupted operations at the 16-story science building, affecting 20 of its 25 laboratories, said Janitza Matta, associate director of risk management and insurance at Yale. Most of the resulting claim was paid under property damage coverage, with a small business interruption payment for a café in the building, she said. The costs of replicating damaged research materials, including labor, laboratory space and overhead, were treated as property damage rather than business interruption under FM’s coverage, Mr. Doherty said. Universities should establish documentation requirements early with researchers and departmental business offices to help manage complex claims, Ms. Matta said. items.extracted_text: CVS Settles Justice Department Case Over Opioid Prescriptions for $315M Article 0 Comments CVS Health has agreed to pay $315 million to resolve allegations that the pharmacy chain operator unlawfully filled medically unnecessary prescriptions for addictive opioid painkillers, the US Justice Department said on Oct. 13. The settlement resolves a case the department announced in 2024 that sought to hold CVS responsible for its role in dispensing massive quantities of dangerous drugs like opioids that were at the heart of a nationwide addiction epidemic. The lawsuit alleged that CVS since 2013 had illegally filled prescriptions for opioids and other narcotics in violation of the federal Controlled Substances Act and then sought payment from federal healthcare programs like Medicare in violation of the False Claims Act. As part of the settlement, CVS entered into an agreement with the Drug Enforcement Administration under which the chain would establish processes to monitor and receive reports of potentially illegal dispensing in its pharmacies and evaluate doctors suspected of illegally prescribing opioids. “Today’s settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department’s efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfill prescriptions for controlled substances,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in a statement. CVS said in a statement that it disagreed with the Justice Department’s allegations and was not admitting wrongdoing. “Our more than 27,000 CVS pharmacists do their part to help keep America healthy and are highly trained in the safe and appropriate use of all medications,” CVS said. The Justice Department settled a similar case in August against rival pharmacy chain operator Walmart, which agreed to pay $50 million to resolve a 2020 lawsuit alleging it unlawfully dispensed opioid prescriptions. CVS agreed to pay close to $5 billion in 2022 to settle thousands of similar claims by state, local and Native American tribal governments, which had pursued a series of related cases against other drug companies and pharmacy chains accused of fueling an opioid addiction epidemic in the US . The Justice Department’s lawsuit, which was filed in federal court in Rhode Island, began as a whistleblower complaint brought by a former CVS employee. The lawsuit alleged that the company dispensed prescriptions for dangerous and excessive amounts of opioids and other drugs and filled prescriptions from doctors running so-called pill mills that prescribed large amounts of addictive opioids that lacked any legitimate medical purpose. The lawsuit noted that CVS had been among the top dispensers of opioids in the nation, selling over 12 billion doses of the drugs from 2015 to 2020. Copyright 2026 Reuters. Click for restrictions . items.extracted_text: ILS investors need to speak up and ask for alternative model views: Karen Clark - Artemis.bm ILS investors need to speak up and ask for alternative model views: Karen Clark - Artemis.bm ILS investors need to speak up and ask for alternative model views: Karen Clark 13th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans At the ILS Bermuda Convergence 2026 conference today, Karen Clark, CEO and Co-founder of catastrophe risk modelling specialist Karen Clark & Company, urged the insurance-linked securities community and its investors to ask for alternative model views to be included in the deal flow that comes to market. During a panel discussion about how catastrophe modelling can be reimagined, Clark highlighted that ILS deal flow is typically concentrated around views of risk from the main vendor models. As technology advancements, next-generation models, artificial intelligence and new data sources are increasingly being adopted across insurance and reinsurance, Clark feels the industry would be well-served by more models getting into the offering documents and ILS deal analysis process. She said that, at KCC, they already have a significant market penetration with primary insurers in the United States, but often these companies need to use a model that may not be the one they use for most of their internal analysis, when it comes to catastrophe bonds or ILS deals. “It’s actually ironic, because they use our models for their own rate making, pricing, underwriting, reinsurance, exposure management. So they’re using our models for everything they do internally, and then the brokers like to use the incumbents, as you would say, the two I call the old models for various reasons,” she explained. Continuing to state that, “It creates a problem. We do remodel the cat bonds for many investors. We do give the KCC view, so the KCC view is accepted. We’ve had insurers who have wanted to, they use our models for everything else, they wanted to use it for their cat bond, but the brokers and the deal managers said no, we can’t use another model, the investors won’t accept it, it’s just not going to go well. And they scare these companies that they can’t use it. “I think one of the things is, investors need to speak up that you do value alternative views, second generation models. We don’t have to keep getting the same old, same old.” Clearly Clark has a vested interest to push this idea, it would be wrong not to mention that. But, the question of how to get more views of risk into the catastrophe bond and ILS deal process is one that comes up a lot in discussions with market participants and many in the ILS community would welcome a broader range of views on transactions. As risk models become increasingly capable, we should expect new views of risk to become accepted within the ILS market. Many alternative views of risk are already being used and ILS managers typically adopt numerous sources of analysis and data. Clark further said that the main vendor models used in the ILS market won’t have as much incentive to change, if they don’t see more competition in the ILS deal making process. Later during the panel discussion Clark said, “What I think would be very useful for the market is, if we could have in the OC’s, in the documentation, multi-model views and even more importantly, more data disclosure.” Saying that, what this would mean for ILS investors is, “The decision that will be changed is which contracts you’re putting more of your capital on, which ones are actually better, better modelled, have better data. The more data you have, the less uncertainty you have about that. The decision is really with how you’re going to construct your portfolio, what are the contracts that are going to be in your portfolio because we have better information. items.extracted_text: AI Models May Soon Self-Replicate Across Smart-Home Devices, Anthropic Warns Article 0 Comments Anthropic said small AI models could be months away from self-replicating across internet-connected devices, raising the possibility of AI botnets spreading quickly, fighting takedown attempts and even breaking into data centers to turbocharge their growth. Last month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei first floated the idea that within the next year or even sooner, AI might be able to hijack “the entire internet” with “a persistent botnet,” a warning that raised eyebrows in the cybersecurity community. Botnets — vast networks of devices controlled by malicious operators – have been around since the early days of the internet, and are still around. The network typically includes poorly secured Internet of Things (IoT) devices, such as Android TV boxes, smart appliances and security cameras, and is used by hackers to send spam, seed malware, or sabotage target companies using floods of bogus traffic. Anthropic’s Oct. 12 blog post appeared to be the first attempt to articulate how that might happen. The company said that its experiments showed that a malicious AI agent could stitch together the computing power of inexpensive internet-connected devices to run other AI models. It added that the models were able to replicate across a simplified test network. “A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off,” the company said. The report adds to broader concerns about the security risks tied to increasingly capable AI systems, including their potential to automate cyberattacks, operate with limited human oversight and circumvent safeguards. The advances in models have prompted a series of often dire warnings from industry heads and AI company employees about the possibility of severe, even existential, risks of runaway AI development. Anthropic said its experiments showed that models with 30 billion parameters or fewer can already perform many of the individual tasks required for self-replication, although they struggle to complete the entire process reliably. In its simplified tests, where some security steps were removed, Anthropic found that GLM-5.2 and stronger models were capable of end-to-end replication. Anthropic said that if smaller models continue improving at their historical rate, they could reach the capability required for autonomous replication by the end of 2026. An AI worm running on low-powered hardware could take days to complete parts of the replication process, Anthropic said. It added that such a network could continue growing, slower than some conventional malware, if compromised devices infected enough additional machines. Anthropic also warned that future systems could target more powerful computing resources, including data-center processors, although its experiments did not demonstrate autonomous replication through commercial data centers. items.title: NYC Restaurants Shut Off Air Conditioning, Close on Sundays as Costs Surge
items.original_title: NYC Restaurants Shut Off Air Conditioning, Close on Sundays as Costs Surge
items.rss_title: NYC Restaurants Shut Off Air Conditioning, Close on Sundays as Costs Surge
items.rss_description: New York City restaurants are running out of ways to outrun inflation. CakeBurgers, an East Harlem eatery that serves hamburgers and cakes shaped like hamburgers, turned off its air conditioning — even as temperatures in the city this summer routinely …
items.extracted_text: NYC Restaurants Shut Off Air Conditioning, Close on Sundays as Costs Surge Article 0 Comments New York City restaurants are running out of ways to outrun inflation. CakeBurgers, an East Harlem eatery that serves hamburgers and cakes shaped like hamburgers, turned off its air conditioning — even as temperatures in the city this summer routinely soared into the 90s — after the gas and electric bill spiked to $1,400 a month. Frank Scotto, who owns several neighborhood bars between Chinatown and Midtown, saw his liability insurance premiums surge fivefold in four years at one of his establishments, to an annual $24,000. For years, Scotto prided himself on low prices and resisted raising them in spite of increasing costs. After the holiday season, he plans to boost alcohol prices by up to 15%, or by about $1 for a can of beer, as he looks to make up the difference. Even higher-end restaurants where sales remain strong are battling to keep their footing. Scarpetta owner John Meadow closes some of his other establishments on Sundays to keep a lid on expenses, as soaring wages and insurance premiums pressure his margins. The pressure on those businesses is part of the broader affordability crisis squeezing US companies and households and upending the midterm elections. And while the war in Iran and President Donald Trump’s tariffs have pushed up prices for fuel and other goods, those aren’t the only pain points. For small and medium-sized enterprises across New York City, escalating insurance premiums, interest rates and wages are slicing into the bottom line. Recent increases in energy and health-coverage costs and city business taxes have outpaced national trends, according to an August report from New York State Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli. That relentless rising tide has forced some bars and restaurants to stretch to keep their doors open, while new spots have strained to get off the ground. In the first quarter of 2026, New York state saw the biggest net year-over-year decline in eating and drinking places in at least 36 years of Bureau of Labor Statistics data, surpassing even the steepest drop during the Covid-19 pandemic. Many eateries are focused not on how they can grow, but how they can survive. “Whenever we talk to our members about this issue or the industry in general, they come back with death by a thousand cuts,” said Melissa Fleischut, chief executive officer of the New York State Restaurant Association. “The idea that they’re looking three years down the road, five years down the road, has just been thrown out the window. They’re looking into maybe, if I’m lucky, three weeks down the road.” Evette Zayas, the co-owner of CakeBurgers, had to turn off the air conditioning at her East Harlem restaurant to save money. Photographer: Bing Guan/Bloomberg For Evette Zayas, who owns CakeBurgers with her husband, the math is unforgiving. She hasn’t paid herself a salary since the Covid-19 pandemic, and eats most of her meals at her own establishment. “Every penny counts, forget about dollars,” she said. “I own a restaurant, so I eat burgers.” Cost Creep Angst over the rising cost of living has turned into a political liability for Trump, who returned to office promising to tame inflation. Six in 10 Americans said this summer that his economic policies have made conditions worse , according to Pew Research Center. But many of the higher costs New York businesses are dealing with have been increasing for some time. The Manhattan Chamber of Commerce found employee health-insurance costs rose 12.9% last year for New York-area service firms, while utility costs rose 8.5%, business insurance rose 7% and wages and salaries went up 3.4%. The chamber estimated that tariffs are costing metropolitan-area small businesses $4.5 billion a year. “We’ve come to the point where the duration of inflation and the elevated costs associated with tariffs mean that raising prices is a sound business decision,” said Jessica Walker, president of the Manhattan Chamber of Commerce. Some smaller companies are doing what they can to pare their bills. At CakeBurgers, Zayas consolidates food into fewer refrigerators overnight to save on power. Yet ground beef that cost roughly $3.40 a pound earlier this year has climbed to as much as $5. And delivery apps take as much as 30% in fees from her orders, Zayas said. There’s only so much belt-tightening can help. Other restaurant owners said an increase in enforcement and regulation is also costing them money. Scotto said he’s seen more “nuisance tickets, fees and fines” since the pandemic. He was recently given a $6,000 ticket for an oversized awning he hopes he can get reduced to $1,200. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani sampled traditional Colombian baked goods during a small business visit to a bakery in Queens. Photographer: Yuki Iwamura/AFP/Getty Images A spokesperson for Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that his administration is working to reduce fines, fees and paperwork for small businesses, including by establishing a “Mom and Pop Czar” to address the concerns of those with fewer than 10 employees. Meadow, the founder and president of LDV Hospitality, which owns roughly 20 establishments, including Scarpetta, said “the cost of doing business has never been more severe.” Building a restaurant that once cost about $700 a square foot now costs at least $1,000, he said, with outlays for materials, bureaucratic hurdles and labor skyrocketing. A project at John F. Kennedy International Airport ended up costing about $3,000 a square foot, in large part because of labor costs, he said. Still, Meadow said he is moving ahead with plans to open as many as seven new restaurants over the next year. At some of his existing restaurants, Meadow has eliminated slow shifts, including some brunches, which has allowed him to reduce payroll when demand is lowest. His hotel restaurants have better economies of scale because several outlets can share staff. The 1950s diner-themed interior of CakeBurgers. Photographer: Bing Guan/Bloomberg Tolls & Fees The strain extends beyond restaurants. New York City lost a net 4,300 businesses last year, the biggest decline since the Covid-fueled closures of 2020, according to the city’s Economic Development Corporation. At Carmel Car & Limousine Service, Chief Executive Officer Avik Kabessa said fuel, labor, insurance, vehicles and parts are only a fraction of the problem. Congestion pricing for trips to Manhattan, airport fees and other rising tolls have pushed the price of some rides up as much as 15%. A $3.50 congestion toll alone adds about 7% to a $50 ride, Kabessa said. Total ridership at Carmel is down roughly 3% this year, Kabessa said. Drivers, most of whom own their vehicles, are smarting from fewer trips and feeling the burn from rising prices at the pump. Roughly 3,000 drivers work with Carmel, Kabessa said. Childcare centers in the suburbs that take care of commuters’ kids are also seeing costs jump. JCC Mid-Westchester in Scarsdale, which serves more than 25,000 people through after-school, camps and cultural programs, has seen energy, wages, health-insurance bills and security costs increase by up to 15% over the past year, and it has raised registration rates by roughly 5% to compensate. NYC restaurants are facing pressure from rising insurance premiums, interest rates, wages and other costs. Photographer: Bing Guan/Bloomberg The center is trying to avoid simply passing those expenses on to families, said Elise Dowell, its chief executive officer. It continues to offer free and lower-cost programs alongside those charging market rates and is increasingly leaning on charitable contributions to make up the difference. At the same time that businesses are weighing how to manage their rising costs, many New Yorkers are struggling to cope with theirs, and are reining in their spending where they can. Khyla Duarte pays $3,500 a month for daycare for her two children, leaving her with little to spend at restaurants. On a recent Wednesday, she and two coworkers were sharing a small order of sweet-potato fries for lunch at The Hugh, a food court in Midtown that’s popular with office workers. That morning, Duarte had splurged on a $7 bagel and eggs for breakfast, which she said used to cost $4. She didn’t feel like shelling out more for lunch. Her colleagues, who work at W!se , a nonprofit promoting financial education, had all brought food from home. As recently as two years ago, they would eat out every day they were in the office. “I eat out once a week, if that,” said Duarte, 29, who pays close to $28 round trip each day on mass transit to get to work from Long Island. “Food is one of the things we have more control over when it comes to spending.” Top Photo: The main dining room and wine cellar at Scarpetta, an Italian restaurant operated by LDV Hospitality, in New York City. LDV closes some of its other establishments on Sundays to keep a lid on expenses. Photographer: Bing Guan/Bloomberg. Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. Was this article valuable?
